messages.text: We’re seeing a lot of drop-off between clicking Pay and getting a response. I’d like to test whether making the waiting state clearer improves purchase conversion.

Right now the button just shows a spinner, so it’s hard to tell whether payment is progressing or stuck. How about a non-modal inline status below the button? Since we can’t calculate a percentage, I’d use indeterminate progress.

That works. One thing, though: a gateway timeout doesn’t mean the payment failed. The payment processor may have approved it even if the response was lost, so I’ll keep the state machine in pending rather than transition it to failed.

Then we shouldn’t send people to an error screen just because it’s taking a while. I’ll start with “Processing your payment” and switch to “Checking your payment status” after a timeout. No optimistic success UI for this flow, either.
What happens if someone refreshes or clicks Pay again while it’s pending? I don’t want the new UI to encourage retries that lead to duplicate charges.

I’ll reuse the same idempotency key for retries of the same payment attempt. On refresh, I’ll restore the state using the existing payment ID. Payment-processor webhooks can arrive more than once, so I’ll dedup by event_id before applying them to the payment state.

Then please keep focus on the button while it’s pending and only block additional submissions. Announce the status copy through a polite live region. I’d rather not move focus on every update or have the screen reader keep announcing the spinner.

Yep. I’ll use aria-disabled instead of native disabled and guard against re-entry in the submit handler. I’ll hide the spinner from the accessibility tree and announce only the status copy. After restoring the payment, I’ll poll with backoff and use the server-verified processor status as the source of truth.
Let’s apply idempotency and state restoration to the control group too. Only the waiting-state presentation should differ in this experiment so we can isolate its effect.

Sounds good. I’ll change only the progress indicator and status copy in the treatment, keeping the button placement and visual hierarchy intact. I’ll expose the error state and retry action only after failure is confirmed.
Please use user-level sticky assignment rather than session-level assignment. The primary metric is purchase CVR among checkout entrants, with AOV and duplicate authorization rate as guardrails.
Then I’ll count conversions from the server-side payment-confirmed event, not the success-screen impression. That way an approved payment won’t be missed just because someone closed the browser.

Yes, let’s use that. I’ll size the sample for a 3% relative MDE. We won’t stop early just because the interim results look good, and if we detect SRM, we’ll hold off on interpreting uplift until we understand the cause.

interpretations.understanding: Test only the payment waiting-state presentation. Keep duplicate-request protection and state recovery in both groups, use persistent user-level assignment and server-confirmed purchases, monitor guardrails, and investigate allocation imbalance before interpreting improvement.

A timeout leaves payment pending. Reuse the payment attempt’s idempotency key, restore its existing state, deduplicate processor events, preserve accessibility and verify the processor status on the server. Count purchases from server payment confirmation.

Use an inline indeterminate waiting state with status copy and no premature success. Preserve keyboard focus, announce status updates politely, keep button placement and visual hierarchy, and show retry only after confirmed failure.
